effect: Association +$8,870 per home (3.0% of median sale price) for the observed average bundle of fronting street trees and nearby crown area; this is not a per-new-tree effect. Keep the tree bundle distinct from a marginal individual tree or a newly planted sapling.

method: Cross-sectional hedonic model; existing trees, not a planting experiment.
authors: Geoffrey H. Donovan and David T. Butry
title: Trees in the city: Valuing street trees in Portland, Oregon
venue: Landscape and Urban Planning 94:77–83; online August 29, 2009.

notes: Source study: Street trees — sales; Cross-sectional hedonic model; existing trees, not a planting experiment.

effect: Association +$21.00 per month per additional street tree at sample means; advertised single-family rents. Craigslist asking rents, not verified signed leases. NIST publication record: https://www.nist.gov/publications/effect-urban-trees-rental-price-single-family-homes-portland-oregon

authors: Geoffrey H. Donovan and David T. Butry
title: The effect of urban trees on the rental price of single-family homes in Portland, Oregon
venue: Urban Forestry & Urban Greening 10; published August 1, 2011.

notes: Source study: Street trees — rents; Cross-sectional semi-log hedonic model.

effect: Association +$1,371 (+0.48%) per 10 percentage-point increase in neighborhood tree cover; includes public and private trees. Not a street-tree-only or planting intervention estimate. Nonlinear specification has diminishing and eventually negative marginal values at high cover. Rural Randolph and Cannon Falls were excluded from the modeled market.
distance: Within 100 m of a home.
authors: Heather Sander, Stephen Polasky and Robert G. Haight
title: The value of urban tree cover: A hedonic property price model in Ramsey and Dakota Counties, Minnesota, USA

notes: Source study: Tree canopy — related to street trees; Spatial hedonic model.

effect: Intervention Approximately +10% in assessed residential values in the year immediately after opening. Primary outcome is assessed building value reflecting rental-income potential. A major rail-to-park conversion in Manhattan; not a generic small-park multiplier. Concurrent redevelopment and development rights are identification concerns discussed by the author.
distance: Within one-third mile of the park.
method: Difference-in-differences with building fixed effects; sales data provide supporting checks.
authors: Michael Levere (December 20, 2014), The High Line Park and Timing of Capitalization of Public Goods. UC San Diego economics working paper; university affiliation and date appear in this version.
quote: Home values within one-third of a mile of the park increased 10% immediately following its opening.
notes: Source study: New parks — High Line; Difference-in-differences with building fixed effects; sales data provide supporting checks.

effect: Intervention +5.4% assessed residential value at 0–250 m; +4.5% at 250–500 m; +6.0% at 500–1,000 m, relative to the 1,000–2,000 m comparison ring. Assessed values, not transaction prices. Distance pattern is not monotonic. The paper acknowledges that measured effects may combine the corridor with related nearby development. Treat this recent study cautiously rather than as a precise transfer coefficient.
distance: 0–250 m; 250–500 m; 500–1,000 m from trail corridor.
method: Parcel and year fixed-effects difference-in-differences/event study.
authors: Duane Ebesu (April 16, 2026), Do Urban Parks Pay for Themselves? Property Value Capitalization and Municipal Fiscal Returns from Chicago’s 606 Trail. Journal of Parks 1(2):8.
quote: …assessed values rise by 5.4%…assessed values rise by 4.5%…assessed values rise by 6.0%.
notes: Source study: New parks — Chicago 606; Parcel and year fixed-effects difference-in-differences/event study.

effect: Intervention +$10,427.58 per home at the mean sale price following playground replacement, in the authors’ capitalization calculation. Replacement is distinct from minor playground renovation. The published 2016 paper has a different title; do not silently attribute this working-paper coefficient to the final version. Effects differ by renovation type and time elapsed.
distance: Within one mile; within four years of completion.
method: Hedonic model with property fixed effects / repeat sales.
authors: Mitchell Livy and H. Allen Klaiber
title: Maintaining Public Goods: Household Valuation of New and Renovated Local Parks
venue: Ohio State University working paper presented at the 2013 AAEA/CAES meeting. These are the 2013 version’s numbers.
quote: …willingness to pay of $10,427.58…within a mile of the renovation, and within four years of the renovation completion date.
notes: Source study: Renovated parks / playground replacement; Hedonic model with property fixed effects / repeat sales.

effect: Intervention Failing to renew maintenance funding: about −11% in year 3, −13% in year 4 and −16% in year 5, relative to barely renewing it. This is a funding-cut effect, not a measured symmetric return to building or renovating a park. Stronger effects for expensive houses and larger levies.
distance: Park/recreation taxing community, not a park-distance band.
method: Regression discontinuity around close renewal elections.
authors: David M. Brasington (June 6, 2023), The effect of open space maintenance spending on house prices. Journal of Regional Science 63(5):1053–1072.
quote: …a drop in house prices of 11% in year 3, 13% in year 4, and 16% in year 5 after the vote.
notes: Source study: Parks — maintenance funding; Regression discontinuity around close renewal elections.

effect: Related evidence Pocket-park-only intervention effect: not found. Related existing community-managed open spaces show +8.69% relative to homes more than half a mile away. CMOS combines play lots, community gardens, memorial gardens and other spaces. It is not an estimate isolated to new pocket parks.
distance: 0–1/8 mile from a community-managed open space.
authors: Sherry Russell and Byoung-Suk Kweon (February 26, 2025), The Economic Effect of Parks and Community-Managed Open Spaces on Residential House Prices in Baltimore, MD. Land 14(3):483.
quote: …CMOS of up to an 1/8 of a mile was 8.69%…
notes: Source study: Pocket parks — closest combined-space evidence; Cross-sectional hedonic model.

effect: Intervention +4.3% after the first year; +13% after six years, then attenuation. Effects vary with neighborhood income, vacancy, crime and nearby pocket parks. They are strongest at moderately high incomes and greater vacancy, with little or no estimated effect at income extremes. Do not treat income as synonymous with market strength.
distance: Within 1,000 ft of a treated vacant lot.
method: Difference-in-differences; hybrid repeat-sales model; matching and propensity-score weighting.
authors: Desen Lin, Shane T. Jensen and Susan M. Wachter (2023; online July 2022), The price effects of greening vacant lots: How neighborhood attributes matter. Real Estate Economics 51:573–610.
quote: …(within 1,000 feet), with a 4.3% rise in value after the first year, and 13% after 6 years (which then attenuates).
notes: Source study: Vacant-lot greening; Difference-in-differences; hybrid repeat-sales model; matching and propensity-score weighting.

effect: Intervention No detectable average capitalization from the demolition program; modest positive effects in areas with low pre-program blight. Distressed Rust Belt market. A statistically undetected average effect does not establish an exact zero or absence of other benefits.
distance: Distance band: not found in the accessible article text.

notes: Source study: Demolition of vacant / blighted buildings; Repeat-sales regression / price indices.

effect: Related evidence +2–5% annual land-price appreciation above a control neighborhood, as reported by the authors; whole-home percentage effect: not found. effect: Intervention +$26.50 in the monthly rental index in treated ZIP codes; citywide rental comparison is statistically insignificant. Short post-launch observation window and ZIP-level indices. A positive treated-ZIP result did not yield a detectable citywide rent effect; not a per-dock multiplier.
distance: ZIP codes containing a bike-share station; no station-radius estimate.
years: January versus July 2015 around the June launch.

quote: This means that the additional increase in the rent price due to the presence of the shared bike system is $26.5.
notes: Source study: Bike share — rents; Difference-in-differences on Zillow ZIP-level rental indices.

effect: Intervention +5–7% in home sale prices. A system-level amenity estimate; do not infer an isolated effect from adding a dedicated bus lane.
distance: Within a 20-minute walk of a station.
method: Difference-in-differences with hedonic and repeat-sales estimators.
authors: Justin Beaudoin and Justin Tyndall (August 19, 2023), The Effect of Bus Rapid Transit on Local Home Prices. University of Hawai‘i UHERO Working Paper 2023-3.
quote: We estimate a 5-7% price premium for homes located within a 20 minute walk of a BRT station.
notes: Source study: Bus rapid transit — Vancouver; Difference-in-differences with hedonic and repeat-sales estimators.

effect: Intervention +41.5% for multifamily residential properties; single-family change not statistically significant. HealthLine is a BRT, streetscape, utility and redevelopment package. A bus-lane-only effect is not found; the large multifamily estimate must not be transferred to all homes.
distance: Within 800 m walking distance of a station.
authors: Blake Acton, Huyen T. K. Le and Harvey J. Miller (March 11, 2022 online), Impacts of bus rapid transit (BRT) on residential property values: A comparative analysis of 11 US BRT systems. Journal of Transport Geography 100:103324.
quote: …with MFR properties appreciating 41.5% while SFR exhibits no significant change.
notes: Source study: Bus rapid transit / dedicated bus lanes — Cleveland; Propensity-score-matched spatial hedonic difference-in-differences.

effect: Intervention Single-family values: Miami −2.5%; Pittsburgh −11.4%. Multifamily changes not statistically significant. Study-specific construction/extension timing, not the opening of Pittsburgh’s entire original busway.
distance: Within 800 m walking distance of a station.
authors: Acton, Le and Miller
title: same paper as the Cleveland row
quote: …both exhibit declines of 2.5% and 11.4% in value respectively…
notes: Source study: Bus rapid transit — busways; Propensity-score-matched spatial hedonic difference-in-differences.

effect: Intervention Neither the funding-announcement nor opening effect is statistically significant; no detectable premium. Mixed-traffic arterial BRT, without the Green Line’s accompanying land-use changes. Lack of a house-price premium does not imply lack of transport benefits.
distance: Within 400 m (¼ mile) of stations.
authors: Jack Lyle Benson and Jason Cao (August 2020), Did the A Line Arterial Bus Rapid Transit Affect Housing Values in Ramsey County, MN? Findings. DOI 10.32866/001c.16628.

effect: Intervention +$9.20 per sq ft after funding announcement; +$13.70 per sq ft by commencement, each relative to the pre-announcement period. These are not additive. Distance and milestone source: https://www.cts.umn.edu/news-pubs/news/2017/june/light-rail . The university notes concurrent streetscape, business-support and zoning changes; pure station-only effect not isolated.
distance: Within ¼ mile of stations.
authors: Xinyu (Jason) Cao and Shengnan Lou (online May 2, 2017; December 2018 issue), When and How Much Did the Green Line LRT Increase Single-Family Housing Values in St. Paul, Minnesota? Journal of Planning Education and Research 38(4):427–436.

notes: Source study: New light-rail stations — Green Line; Before/after treatment-control hedonic difference-in-differences.

effect: Intervention +6.8%, immediate and largely permanent, in the main difference-in-differences estimate. Smaller gains farther away. notes: Source study: Freeway noise walls; Spatial difference-in-differences; proposed-but-unbuilt barriers support a separate triple-difference check.

effect: Intervention +7% at 0–399.9 m; approximately +4% at 400–800 m after opening, relative to more distant comparable homes. Stores were generally in lower-value neighborhoods. notes: Source study: New supermarkets / grocery stores; Difference-in-differences hedonic model; placebo opening-year tests.

My assessment: the prose’s percentage interpretation conflicts with the log-model coefficients, so I have not transcribed a percentage as a usable project effect. Selection into Main Street participation is also acknowledged by the author.

Prices fell after formal adoption; this is not a permanent post-adoption uplift. Anticipation and prior price trends complicate causal interpretation. Commercial-property gains reported elsewhere in this paper are not substituted for home-price effects.
distance: Inside BID boundaries versus surrounding properties; no universal distance band.

notes: Source study: Business improvement districts — residential outcomes; Hedonic difference-in-differences with pre-adoption trends and boundary comparisons.

effect: Intervention +10.3% in home values in neighborhoods assigned to new or substantially renovated elementary/middle schools. A bond-authorization-only effect is not isolated. notes: Source study: School facility investments / bonds; Difference-in-differences exploiting staggered school construction and neighborhood fixed effects.
